newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. Gov says state no longer a 'welfare magnet'.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. Gov says state no longer a 'welfare magnet'.

text.p: New York Gov. George Pataki said the major changes for welfare that he has agreed with Albany lawmakers mean poor people no longer will want to move to the state to collect its rich benefits.

The preliminary 1998 fiscal budget would end the state's cash benefits for residents after two years -- a lifetime limit -- after which they would get non-cash benefits with a small, personal needs allowence, the governor said Tuesday.

Pataki, who says the state has cut its welfare rolls by more than 350,000 since 1995, was unable to get Assembly Democrats to agree to gradually cut federal welfare cash benefits over five years. Washington's new welfare system gives states considerable flexibility in setting up their programs, though it requires states to enroll welfare recipients in workfare programs and ends cash benefits after five years.

New York State lawmakers agreed that after the federal welfare program ends, the needy would qualify for non-cash services provided through a debit card. Only 20 percent of their aid would paid in cash, local newspapers said on Wednesday. Newsday said that swipecard systems will be installed free in retail shops through-out the state.

However, the Assembly was unable to get Pataki to approve paying workfare participants the prevailing wage if it were higher than the minimum wage. The new federal budget that was preliminarily agreed calls for paying workfare participants the minimum wage, a policy Pataki had fought as too costly.

People who collected welfare benefits would, however, be allowed to keep more of what they earned from other jobs, a policy that was pushed by a number of advocates for the poor. Recipients would be able to keep $1,080, up from the present limit of $667, before their welfare benefits were stopped. And individuals who left the welfare rolls because they found jobs still could get Medicaid and child care benefits for up to one year, along with subsidies for low-income daycare.

Still, the Republican governor said he defeated the Assembly's plans to let workfare participants unionize and eventually gain the same status as public employees, qualifying for benefits, like vacation.

Despite a controversy over the death of a New York City workfare participant, who had a heart condition, Pataki added he turned back demands for more liberal definitions of disability in the Americans with Disabilities Act. That change, which was sought by the Assembly, would have exempted more individuals from workfare.

The New York Times, in its Wednesday edition, said anyone who was too ill to work, including those were HIV positive, could get cash benefits without any time limits. It added those who were not eligible for cash benefits could get emergency aid for essentials, like food or clothing, through a mix of cash and debit cards.

Individuals who moved to New York State in the first year would only get 50 percent of the state benefit or the amount they would get in the state they left. And legal immigrants, during their first year in the state, would get non-cash benefits with a small, personal needs allowence. After that, they would qualify for New York State's two-year cash program. When that ended, they would fall under the non-cash plan.

"The abolition of the state's Home Relief program, which provided cash benefits and the creation of a new Safety Net program that provides non-cash benefits will help ensure that the people who come to New York are here to work and not to take advantage of our compassion," Pataki said, in prepared remarks released late Tuesday.

The New York Times also said advocates for the poor criticized the state's new welfare plan for unfairly denying recipients decent payment levels and the right to unionize, and for forcing them to shop at stores that would accept their vouchers even if those stores charged higher prices.
